newsitem.title: ITALY: Court acquits Italians of American boy's murder.
newsitem.headline: Court acquits Italians of American boy's murder.

text.p: Two Italians were cleared on Thursday of murdering a seven-year-old American boy who became a symbol of compassion in Italy when his parents donated his organs to save seven lives.
A court in Catanzaro, southern Italy, acquitted Francesco Mesiano, 23 and Michele Iannello, 28, of murder for the shooting death of Nicholas Green during an attempted motorway robbery.
Both defendants had denied the charges. The prosecution had asked the court to impose prison terms of 23 years.
Nicholas was on holiday with his family, from Bodega Bay, California, when their hired car was chased and shot at on an isolated stretch of motorway in the southern Calabria region in September 1994.
He was hit in the head as he slept on the back seat next to his sister, who was then four, and died two days later.

The verdict was announced as Italians remained transfixed by another senseless act of highway violence, the killing of a newly-wed woman in northern Italy on December 27 when a rock was thrown at her car from a bridge.
Three brothers were arrested in connection with the killing on Thursday and questioned by magistrates in a court building where a hundreds-strong crowd gathered to bay for punishment.
In Catanzaro, Mesiano cried when the verdict was read. He later approached the boy's father, Reginald, in the courtroom and offered his hand, which Green accepted and shook.
Green told reporters he felt the trial had been conducted "scrupulously and meticulously", adding: "The charges were reasoned and professional and now the court has reached its conclusions".
"A car came out of the dark and approached us. It was very difficult to prove anything," he said.

Green and his wife Margaret, who recently had twin girls, earned deep respect in Italy, where organ donation is rare. Shocked by the killing of a young boy, Italians were touched by the couple's apparent lack of rancour.

The media praised them as humanitarian heroes, President Oscar Luigi Scalfaro gave them a medal and they left the country after the shooting with pledges that hospitals, streets and schools would be named after their son.
Mesiano and Iannello had been charged with Nicholas's murder about a month after the shooting.

Soon after his arrest, Iannello turned state's evidence and supplied information to police about four other murders while steadfastly denying he had anything to do with Nicholas's death. He is living under a witness protection scheme.

The court, which took five hours to reach a verdict, had released Mesiano from jail into house arrest a month ago after he complained of violent headaches, back problems and anxiety attacks. He was freed after the verdict.
